REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizen of Nigeria (Nigerian passport submitted), is claiming refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

[2] In rendering my reasons, I have considered and applied the Chairperson's Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.
CLAIMANT'S ALLEGATIONS

[3] The claimant is 34 and is married to a XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria. They adopted a daughter.

[4] On XXXX XXXX 2017, while living in Ekiti (Ekiti State), she received a threatening letter that had written "we are watching your family" and listed her two residence addresses, one in Ekiti State and one in Ondo State. She and her husband did not understand why they would receive such a letter.

[5] The next day, they received another threatening letter warning her husband not to be involved in that XXXX, or else the claimant's family will have to bear the consequences. The author of the letter was still unknown, but the claimant, scared for the safety of her family, begged her husband to XXXX XXXX XXXX he believed provoked the threats. He refused, calling the threats baseless. The claimant decided to go into hiding with her daughter and she decided to report the matter to the police.

[6] On XXXX XXXX (2017), before making a report to the police, the claimant and her husband received another threatening letter, this one with a picture of a casket, that read if the claimant or her husband go to the police, the aggressors will kill them (the husband, wife, family) faster, and the letter listed the name of the daughter's school.

[7] The claimant and the daughter went to hide in Kogi State in XXXX (2017).

[8] On XXXX XXXX 2017, the claimant received at her home a picture of an axe and red cloth attached to her door. She returned to Ekiti State to report her insecurities.

[9] Upon return to her home area in Ekiti, there were government officials all around, houses were being destroyed, cars damaged, fire, and people running for their lives. The claimant was grabbed by an officer in uniform, then found herself in the bush after having lost consciousness. She did not know what might have happened to her in that bush on that day.

[10] She then ran to Ondo State. She had no money, since she was completely robbed. A red cloth was dropped in her bag.

[11] On XXXX XXXX (2017), the claimant and her daughter went to Oyo State, where she left her daughter with a sister, and then went to Lagos on XXXX XXXX, where she took a plane to the United States (US), and then to Canada to make a refugee claim.

[34] I asked the claimant at both sittings of the hearing what efforts she had made to produce as evidence those articles and other evidence in support of her claim. I emphasized the importance of these articles as a possible means of showing who was threatening her and her husband, that the claimant's husband was involved in those XXXX, and that the claimant and her husband are in a similar situation of potential harm as the colleagues harmed. The claimant responded that her husband's situation is unstable and that he was unable to get the media reports. Asked why her husband could not get the media reports if he had provided so many other documents (some of them very recently, in 2019), the claimant responded that he has not been well recently, and testified elsewhere in the hearing that he is living as a nomad and has stopped work.

She testified that she is in communication with her husband almost daily, and did not adequately explain why she could not simply ask her husband for more details concerning the news articles and obtain them herself from the sources. I note that the NDP makes multiple references to the media sources the Nation, Vanguard, and the Punch as being major credible Nigerian news sources with Internet sites.
Threatening Letters

[36] The claimant and her counsel listed six threatening letters in the table of contents of the submitted evidence of 24 April 2019. The tribunal only received two photocopies of threatening letters in the documents received dated 24 April 2019. On the day of the hearing, the claimant submitted six original threatening letters with red "X" at the bottom (C-7). One of the threatening letters (C-7.1b), submitted to the tribunal as the original of a photocopy of the same threatening letter already submitted into evidence (C-7.1a), did not match the copy. It is not the same document: C-7.1b has two white triangles in the image of the coffin and the handwritten "X" at the bottom is not the same as in C-7.1a.

[37] I asked the claimant why there was a difference between the two documents. She responded that she did not know.

[38] Asked why she would not have submitted the four other threatening letters on 24 April 2019 with the two others, the claimant responded that the two letters were the ones available to her at the time, and she testified that she or her husband had received five threatening letters together in total, and one letter was found with the dead body of her husband's brother, making a total of six threatening letters.

[39] The claimant's explanation for the difference between C-7.1b and C-7.1a is not adequate, and undermines her credibility and reliability as a witness able to submit original documents in support of photocopy evidence that she submitted. She submitted C-7.1b as the original of C-7.1a, since it is the only threatening letter with a coffin in it and there are only six threatening letters, according to her testimony. However, with C-7.1b and C-7.1a being two separate documents, there are in effect seven threatening letters. Having considered all of the evidence and finding the claimant generally not credible, and with her inadequate explanation for the non-corresponding threatening letter, C-7.1b, I conclude that she has submitted a fraudulent document into evidence in her refugee claim.

[40] Since all of the threatening letters of a similar style and source, because one or more of them is fraudulent, and because the claimant is generally not credible, I do not give any probative value to any of them.
Police report of XXXX XXXX 2018

[41] During the hearing of 8 May 2019, I requested from counsel and the claimant the first pages of C-9, because it appeared that I had only received the last two pages, including the officer's signature at the end on 24 April 2019. Counsel gave me a photocopy of all the pages of C-9 for the refugee file.

[42] At that same sitting of the hearing, the claimant submitted an original police report dated XXXX XXXX 2018 (C-9b), which did not match the photocopy of the same alleged document submitted earlier into evidence (C-9a) sent to our file on 24 April 2019. At the subsequent sitting of the hearing, on 28 May 2019, I mentioned that the two documents do not appear to be the same and asked the claimant first if the original she submitted of C-9 was the same as the photocopy of C-9 that she submitted. She responded that they are the same words, and the one she submitted at the hearing is the true copy of the original and the photocopy was a scanned copy. Asked if the scanned copy of C-9 in our file was a copy of the original, she responded that the scanned copy was not supposed to be used and that the original is the true copy. Asked if there are two versions of the document, the claimant responded that a drink spilled on it and another one was done.

[43] Asked why she would not have mentioned earlier, on presentation of the original of C-9, that the original was not the same document as the C-9 photocopy, the claimant responded that she should have mentioned it, but did not.

[44] C-9a photocopy had only the last two pages of a four-page document, and the last page was highly pixelated and showed the signature in a different position and the word order of the address at the bottom of the page in a different order compared to the original C-9b. Also, the first three pages of C-9a, which were eventually received in the hearing file on 8 May 2019, were very clear compared to the last signature page, that was highly pixelated on page 4 of C-9a, which does not appear to be from the same document as the first three pages of C-9a, based on the quality of the image, scan or photocopy.

[45] The claimant's explanation for the difference between C-9a and C-9b is not adequate, and undermines her credibility and reliability as a witness able to submit original documents in support of photocopy evidence that she submitted. She submitted C-9b as the original of C-9a, as if they were the same document. Having considered all of the evidence and finding the claimant generally not credible, and with her inadequate explanation of the non-corresponding original, C-9b, I conclude that she has submitted a fraudulent document into evidence in her refugee claim.
Other Documentary Evidence

[46] The claimant submitted a photocopy of her marriage certificate (original not available) and photos of her wedding (C-14 and C-15). I had no particular reason to doubt that the claimant was married as she alleged. The marriage certificate shows that her husband is a XXXX.

[47] Documents referring to her husband's XXXX XXXX or XXXX were submitted (C-4 and C-6). I accept that the claimant's husband is or was a XXXX in Nigeria.

[48] A letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was submitted, dated XXXX XXXX 2019 (C-5), from the XXXX XXXX. The document attests that the claimant's husband can XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria, and that he stopped due to threats or attacks against him and/or his family and recommends protection. The document does not show that the author has independent knowledge of specific attacks and threats against the claimant's husband, other than what her husband would have told the author (XXXX XXXX). Given that, after having considered all of the evidence, I find the claimant generally not credible and some of her evidence fraudulent, and related to events directly involving the claimant's husband, I conclude that the husband is not a reliable or credible witness. Consequently, since it has not been shown that the XXXX XXXX is relying on information other than the declaration of the husband, I conclude that the XXXX letter does not have any probative value.

[49] The claimant submitted an affidavit from her husband dated XXXX XXXX 2019 (C-13), where he alleges that his brother was assassinated by unknown gunmen. For the reasons stated above for finding the claimant's husband not reliable or credible as a witness, I find that his affidavit does not have any probative value.

[50] The death certificate of the husband's brother (C-3) does not show the cause of death, and is not probative evidence that the cause of the death was the aggressors that the claimant alleges are threatening her. The alleged photo of the brother-in-law (C-16) relies on the claimant's testimony describing the photo as being that of her assassinated brother-in-law, and since I find her generally not credible as a witness, the photo does not have any probative value as proof of the brother's violent death or that he was killed by the same aggressors targeting the claimant.

[51] The claimant submitted a photo (C-8) of her husband with a bandage over his right eye. The claimant testified that her husband was attacked by the aggressors targeting them and he nearly lost an eye. The photo on its own is not probative evidence of the cause of the injury and since the cause of the injury relies on the claimant's explanation of the cause and, after having considered all of the evidence, I find her generally not credible, the photo does not have probative as evidence in support of her allegations.

[52] The signing officer's name in C-9 is XXXX, and the Nigerian police stamp that appears at the bottom of the last page also appears in the death report to the coroner for the husband's brother's death (C-2). Since I conclude that C-9 is a fraudulent document and the signing officers are the same in C-2 as in C-9, I do not give any probative value to C-2.

[53] I note that the NDP mentions that fraudulent documents are common in Nigeria1 in relation to fake news, affidavits from the court, and corrupt state officials. Therefore, in conjunction with the claimant's general lack of credibility, there is serious reason to doubt the credibility and probative value of the submitted documents.
Claim is Manifestly Unfounded

[54] Section 107.1 of the IRPA reads:
"If the Refugee Protection Division rejects a claim for refugee protection, it must state in its reasons for the decision that the claim is manifestly unfounded if it is of the opinion that the claim is clearly fraudulent."

[55] I understand "clearly fraudulent" to include where a refugee claimant is deliberately attempting to deceive the tribunal in a refugee claim. I do not consider that a claim is "clearly fraudulent" if, in spite of false statements from a claimant, there is other credible and probative evidence showing the well-foundedness of the claim. I consider that the claimant's false allegations or misrepresentation of alleged fact must be material or of substantive nature relevant to the claim, in order for the claim to be considered "clearly fraudulent".

[56] After having considered the totality of the evidence (the claimant's testimony, personal written statements, and other evidence), I conclude that the claimant is generally not credible as a witness. For the reasons already stated above, I find that the documentary evidence is insufficiently credible and probative to support the claimant's allegations of past and future harm in Nigeria.

[26] The claimant's explanation is not adequate and weakens her credibility regarding threats being made against her in Nigeria and when those threats began. I am aware that in the police report dated XXXX XXXX 2018 (C-10), it is mentioned that the husband received threats and attacks starting in XXXX 2017, which extended to his family in XXXX 2017. However, the claimant, in her response, did not deny that she was the subject of threats from the same aggressors starting in XXXX 2017, as implied in the earlier police report (C-9a and C-9b).

[27] The claimant's husband alleged in his affidavit (C-12) that he had received a serious life threatening message in XXXX 2017, but did not tell his wife (the claimant), to avoid scaring her. But later in the same affidavit, he mentions that later, in XXXX 2017, "we", he and his wife, received another dreadful and threatening note on XXXX XXXX 2017, and that later in XXXX (2017), he and the claimant decided to report the matter to the police.

[28] The claimant declared in her BOC that after she received two threatening letters in relation to her husband's XXXX XXXX, on XXXX and XXXX XXXX 2017, she immediately, on XXXX XXXX 2017, informed her husband of the threats, but he did not take the threats to him or her seriously, calling it bogus and baseless.

[29] I asked the claimant why she thought her husband would call the new threats in XXXX 2017 bogus and baseless, as she stated in her BOC, if her husband referred to those same threats as dreadful and from the same persons who had communicated to him serious threats to life in XXXX 2017. She responded repeating what she had written in her BOC, that her husband did not want to scare her.

[30] The claimant's explanation is not adequate and weakens her credibility regarding threats being made against her in Nigeria. If her husband told her that the threats she and he received in XXXX 2017 were bogus and baseless, then I would expect that there would be some indication in his affidavit (C-12) that he wanted to minimize the perception of danger to reassure his wife (so she would not be scared), as he had done in XXXX 2017, where he stated that he did not mention the threats at all to his wife at first. XXXX XXXX - Staple Marks - Internet Version Not Submitted in Either Sitting

[31] The claimant submitted an article from XXXX XXXX dated XXXX 2019 (C-11). She showed the original document in the hearing room and I made a photocopy of additional pages of the magazine. The magazine had an article on her husband being the subject of threats in Nigeria because of his XXXX XXXX. The claimant testified that the magazine is available on the Internet through the publisher, XXXX XXXX XXXX (C-17). Asked what efforts she made to submit into evidence a document showing or proving that the magazine exists on the Internet at the subsequent sitting of the hearing, the claimant simply responded that it is available (not providing document evidence), and provided a new document article from the XXXX XXXX on her husband being the subject of threats in Nigeria because of his XXXX XXXX (C-18). However, the claimant did not provide other evidence to show that this publication is available on the Internet, other than a handwritten Internet address that I tried to access on the Internet, but I was unsuccessful. The XXXX XXXX is not mentioned in the NDP.

[32] The claimant's efforts to show that the two above publications exist as credible news sources with wide circulation are not adequate. The documents do not have any probative value as evidence, and have not been shown to be independent publications beyond the influence and control of the claimant or her husband.
Efforts to Obtain the News Articles in Nigeria Newspapers, the Nation, Vanguard, and Punch

[33] The claimant's husband wrote, in his statements to the police (C-10) and in his affidavit (C-12), that he had been involved in XXXX XXXX as a XXXX XXXX XXXX, which may be the reason he and his wife were targeted for threats and attacks, and that those XXXX XXXX were reported in several news articles in Nigerian newspapers, the Nation, Vanguard, and Punch. The husband's statements are specific with regard to the existence of these articles, giving the dates of the articles and other colleagues involved in those same XXXX who have been attacked, kidnapped, or assassinated.

[34] I asked the claimant at both sittings of the hearing what efforts she had made to produce as evidence those articles and other evidence in support of her claim. I emphasized the importance of these articles as a possible means of showing who was threatening her and her husband, that the claimant's husband was involved in those XXXX, and that the claimant and her husband are in a similar situation of potential harm as the colleagues harmed. The claimant responded that her husband's situation is unstable and that he was unable to get the media reports. Asked why her husband could not get the media reports if he had provided so many other documents (some of them very recently, in 2019), the claimant responded that he has not been well recently, and testified elsewhere in the hearing that he is living as a nomad and has stopped work.

[35] The claimant's explanation is not adequate, and weakens her credibility regarding the existence of these news articles from major Nigerian news sources that have been alleged to show that the claimant's husband, as a XXXX XXXX XXXX, has been involved in XXXX XXXX XXXX that may threaten him and the claimant. She testified that she is in communication with her husband almost daily, and did not adequately explain why she could not simply ask her husband for more details concerning the news articles and obtain them herself from the sources. I note that the NDP makes multiple references to the media sources the Nation, Vanguard, and the Punch as being major credible Nigerian news sources with Internet sites.
Threatening Letters

[41] During the hearing of 8 May 2019, I requested from counsel and the claimant the first pages of C-9, because it appeared that I had only received the last two pages, including the officer's signature at the end on 24 April 2019. [42] At that same sitting of the hearing, the claimant submitted an original police report dated XXXX XXXX 2018 (C-9b), which did not match the photocopy of the same alleged document submitted earlier into evidence (C-9a) sent to our file on 24 April 2019. At the subsequent sitting of the hearing, on 28 May 2019, I mentioned that the two documents do not appear to be the same and asked the claimant first if the original she submitted of C-9 was the same as the photocopy of C-9 that she submitted. She responded that they are the same words, and the one she submitted at the hearing is the true copy of the original and the photocopy was a scanned copy. Asked if there are two versions of the document, the claimant responded that a drink spilled on it and another one was done.

[43] Asked why she would not have mentioned earlier, on presentation of the original of C-9, that the original was not the same document as the C-9 photocopy, the claimant responded that she should have mentioned it, but did not.

[44] C-9a photocopy had only the last two pages of a four-page document, and the last page was highly pixelated and showed the signature in a different position and the word order of the address at the bottom of the page in a different order compared to the original C-9b. Having considered all of the evidence and finding the claimant generally not credible, and with her inadequate explanation of the non-corresponding original, C-9b, I conclude that she has submitted a fraudulent document into evidence in her refugee claim.
Other Documentary Evidence

[46] The claimant submitted a photocopy of her marriage certificate (original not available) and photos of her wedding (C-14 and C-15). I had no particular reason to doubt that the claimant was married as she alleged. The marriage certificate shows that her husband is a XXXX.

[47] Documents referring to her husband's XXXX XXXX or XXXX were submitted (C-4 and C-6). I accept that the claimant's husband is or was a XXXX in Nigeria.

[48] A letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was submitted, dated XXXX XXXX 2019 (C-5), from the XXXX XXXX. The document attests that the claimant's husband can XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria, and that he stopped due to threats or attacks against him and/or his family and recommends protection. The document does not show that the author has independent knowledge of specific attacks and threats against the claimant's husband, other than what her husband would have told the author (XXXX XXXX). Given that, after having considered all of the evidence, I find the claimant generally not credible and some of her evidence fraudulent, and related to events directly involving the claimant's husband, I conclude that the husband is not a reliable or credible witness. Consequently, since it has not been shown that the XXXX XXXX is relying on information other than the declaration of the husband, I conclude that the XXXX letter does not have any probative value.

[49] The claimant submitted an affidavit from her husband dated XXXX XXXX 2019 (C-13), where he alleges that his brother was assassinated by unknown gunmen. For the reasons stated above for finding the claimant's husband not reliable or credible as a witness, I find that his affidavit does not have any probative value.

[50] The death certificate of the husband's brother (C-3) does not show the cause of death, and is not probative evidence that the cause of the death was the aggressors that the claimant alleges are threatening her. The alleged photo of the brother-in-law (C-16) relies on the claimant's testimony describing the photo as being that of her assassinated brother-in-law, and since I find her generally not credible as a witness, the photo does not have any probative value as proof of the brother's violent death or that he was killed by the same aggressors targeting the claimant.

[52] The signing officer's name in C-9 is XXXX, and the Nigerian police stamp that appears at the bottom of the last page also appears in the death report to the coroner for the husband's brother's death (C-2). Claim is Manifestly Unfounded

[54] Section 107.1 of the IRPA reads:

[57] In particular, I consider that the claimant has submitted fraudulent documents, either documents that are fake, or authentic documents created in a fraudulent manner and not according to accepted laws or rules of a country. [58] I conclude from the above that the claimant intentionally attempted to deceive the panel regarding documentary evidence central and material to the claim, and that her claim is clearly fraudulent and manifestly unfounded.
CONCLUSION

[59] I therefore reject your claim under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA, and I further find that your claim is manifestly unfounded pursuant to section 107.1 of the IRPA.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizen of Nigeria (Nigerian passport submitted), is claiming refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

[2] In rendering my reasons, I have considered and applied the Chairperson's Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.
CLAIMANT'S ALLEGATIONS
[3] The claimant is 34 and is married to a XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria. They adopted a daughter.

[4] On XXXX XXXX 2017, while living in Ekiti (Ekiti State), she received a threatening letter that had written "we are watching your family" and listed her two residence addresses, one in Ekiti State and one in Ondo State. She and her husband did not understand why they would receive such a letter.

[5] The next day, they received another threatening letter warning her husband not to be involved in that XXXX, or else the claimant's family will have to bear the consequences. The author of the letter was still unknown, but the claimant, scared for the safety of her family, begged her husband to XXXX XXXX XXXX he believed provoked the threats. He refused, calling the threats baseless. The claimant decided to go into hiding with her daughter and she decided to report the matter to the police.

[6] On XXXX XXXX (2017), before making a report to the police, the claimant and her husband received another threatening letter, this one with a picture of a casket, that read if the claimant or her husband go to the police, the aggressors will kill them (the husband, wife, family) faster, and the letter listed the name of the daughter's school.
[7] The claimant and the daughter went to hide in Kogi State in XXXX (2017).
[8] On XXXX XXXX 2017, the claimant received at her home a picture of an axe and red cloth attached to her door. She returned to Ekiti State to report her insecurities.

[9] Upon return to her home area in Ekiti, there were government officials all around, houses were being destroyed, cars damaged, fire, and people running for their lives. The claimant was grabbed by an officer in uniform, then found herself in the bush after having lost consciousness. She did not know what might have happened to her in that bush on that day.
[10] She then ran to Ondo State. She had no money, since she was completely robbed. A red cloth was dropped in her bag.

[11] On XXXX XXXX (2017), the claimant and her daughter went to Oyo State, where she left her daughter with a sister, and then went to Lagos on XXXX XXXX, where she took a plane to the United States (US), and then to Canada to make a refugee claim.
[12] After arriving in Canada on 14 October 2017, her daughter was followed by a strange man who wanted to take her to some place. The daughter refused and shouted.
[13] The claimant's husband is living as a nomad, constantly changing his hiding place.

[14] In a Basis of Claim form (BOC) narrative update, dated 23 April 2019, the claimant further alleged that on XXXX XXXX 2017, she was raped by unknown men in police uniforms, and added that she did not write this down at first, because she was too ashamed to disclose it even to her husband. But then, her husband received a blackmail letter threatening to publish nude pictures of her that had been sent to her husband.

[15] On XXXX XXXX 2018, her husband's brother was assassinated in her husband's car in Lagos by the same threatening unknown gunmen. A threatening letter was found with the body, threatening revenge on the claimant's family.

[16] The claimant's husband was attacked and injured by the same unknown men in Port Harcourt on XXXX XXXX 2017, and he lives as a nomad and stopped his XXXX XXXX due to the threats and insecurity.
DETERMINATION

[17] I find that you have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities, you would be personally subjected to a risk to life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture, upon return to your country.
ANALYSIS
Credibility

[18] I note that the claimant completed her BOC in English without an interpreter and testified during the hearing mostly in English, without an interpreter. She declared in her Schedule A form that she completed at least five years of university or college studies in XXXX and XXXX and worked as a XXXX XXXX from 2009 to XXXX 2017.

[19] In assessing the claimant's credibility, I am particularly conscious of the Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution, in particular section D, referring to women reluctant to disclose their experiences of sexual violence for reason of shame, or to maintain dignity according to cultural norms, and the symptoms of rape trauma syndrome, such as difficulty concentrating and memory loss or distortion.

[20] Consequently, the claimant's explanation for the late disclosure of an alleged rape is a reasonable and acceptable one. She testified clearly that the persons who sexually assaulted her, she believed, were not government authorities or the police, but rather persons "disguised" in uniforms.

[21] However, regarding the other incongruities in her testimony or evidence, she has not referred to shock, trauma or psychological problems as being the cause and the evidence does not show that difficulty in concentrating or memory were affected by a past assault that would explain these incongruities, contradictions or omissions.
[22] The claimant testified during the hearing with confidence and without hesitation.

[23] I find her testimony not to be credible with respect to the following areas.
Threats of XXXX XXXX 2017

[24] The claimant testified that she received the first of a series of threats in XXXX 2017, when she received a threatening letter, as she had stated in her BOC. However, she had submitted a BOC narrative update on 24 April 2019, when she had also submitted evidence that her husband, in the police report dated XXXX XXXX 2018 (C-9a and C-9b), stated to the police that he and his family members (that would include his wife, the claimant) were facing or received threats and attacks from a group of unknown persons since XXXX 2017.

[25] I asked the claimant, even if she only learned after XXXX 2017 about threats being made against her by the same aggressors starting in XXXX 2017, why she would not have mentioned in her BOC narrative update, for example, that she was the target of these threats starting in XXXX 2017 rather than in XXXX 2017. She responded that she was concentrating on her and what happened to her. Asked what threats would have been made against her husband's family members in XXXX 2017, as mentioned in C-9a and C-9b, she responded that she does not have any knowledge of that.

[26] The claimant's explanation is not adequate and weakens her credibility regarding threats being made against her in Nigeria and when those threats began. I am aware that in the police report dated XXXX XXXX 2018 (C-10), it is mentioned that the husband received threats and attacks starting in XXXX 2017, which extended to his family in XXXX 2017. However, the claimant, in her response, did not deny that she was the subject of threats from the same aggressors starting in XXXX 2017, as implied in the earlier police report (C-9a and C-9b).

[27] The claimant's husband alleged in his affidavit (C-12) that he had received a serious life threatening message in XXXX 2017, but did not tell his wife (the claimant), to avoid scaring her. But later in the same affidavit, he mentions that later, in XXXX 2017, "we", he and his wife, received another dreadful and threatening note on XXXX XXXX 2017, and that later in XXXX (2017), he and the claimant decided to report the matter to the police.

[28] The claimant declared in her BOC that after she received two threatening letters in relation to her husband's XXXX XXXX, on XXXX and XXXX XXXX 2017, she immediately, on XXXX XXXX 2017, informed her husband of the threats, but he did not take the threats to him or her seriously, calling it bogus and baseless.

[29] I asked the claimant why she thought her husband would call the new threats in XXXX 2017 bogus and baseless, as she stated in her BOC, if her husband referred to those same threats as dreadful and from the same persons who had communicated to him serious threats to life in XXXX 2017. She responded repeating what she had written in her BOC, that her husband did not want to scare her.

[30] The claimant's explanation is not adequate and weakens her credibility regarding threats being made against her in Nigeria. If her husband told her that the threats she and he received in XXXX 2017 were bogus and baseless, then I would expect that there would be some indication in his affidavit (C-12) that he wanted to minimize the perception of danger to reassure his wife (so she would not be scared), as he had done in XXXX 2017, where he stated that he did not mention the threats at all to his wife at first. There is no indication in the affidavit (C-12) that he did not take the threats of XXXX 2017 seriously, or that he tried to convince his wife that they were not serious.
XXXX XXXX - Staple Marks - Internet Version Not Submitted in Either Sitting

[31] The claimant submitted an article from XXXX XXXX dated XXXX 2019 (C-11). She showed the original document in the hearing room and I made a photocopy of additional pages of the magazine. The magazine had an article on her husband being the subject of threats in Nigeria because of his XXXX XXXX. The name of this magazine does not appear in the National Documentation Package for Nigeria (NDP), dated 30 April 2019. The claimant testified that the magazine is available on the Internet through the publisher, XXXX XXXX XXXX (C-17). I note that in the publisher information for the magazine, there is an email address, but no Internet address for the magazine. Asked what efforts she made to submit into evidence a document showing or proving that the magazine exists on the Internet at the subsequent sitting of the hearing, the claimant simply responded that it is available (not providing document evidence), and provided a new document article from the XXXX XXXX on her husband being the subject of threats in Nigeria because of his XXXX XXXX (C-18). However, the claimant did not provide other evidence to show that this publication is available on the Internet, other than a handwritten Internet address that I tried to access on the Internet, but I was unsuccessful. The XXXX XXXX is not mentioned in the NDP.

[32] The claimant's efforts to show that the two above publications exist as credible news sources with wide circulation are not adequate. The documents do not have any probative value as evidence, and have not been shown to be independent publications beyond the influence and control of the claimant or her husband.
Efforts to Obtain the News Articles in Nigeria Newspapers, the Nation, Vanguard, and Punch

[33] The claimant's husband wrote, in his statements to the police (C-10) and in his affidavit (C-12), that he had been involved in XXXX XXXX as a XXXX XXXX XXXX, which may be the reason he and his wife were targeted for threats and attacks, and that those XXXX XXXX were reported in several news articles in Nigerian newspapers, the Nation, Vanguard, and Punch. The husband's statements are specific with regard to the existence of these articles, giving the dates of the articles and other colleagues involved in those same XXXX who have been attacked, kidnapped, or assassinated.

[34] I asked the claimant at both sittings of the hearing what efforts she had made to produce as evidence those articles and other evidence in support of her claim. I emphasized the importance of these articles as a possible means of showing who was threatening her and her husband, that the claimant's husband was involved in those XXXX, and that the claimant and her husband are in a similar situation of potential harm as the colleagues harmed. The claimant responded that her husband's situation is unstable and that he was unable to get the media reports. Asked why her husband could not get the media reports if he had provided so many other documents (some of them very recently, in 2019), the claimant responded that he has not been well recently, and testified elsewhere in the hearing that he is living as a nomad and has stopped work.

[35] The claimant's explanation is not adequate, and weakens her credibility regarding the existence of these news articles from major Nigerian news sources that have been alleged to show that the claimant's husband, as a XXXX XXXX XXXX, has been involved in XXXX XXXX XXXX that may threaten him and the claimant. She testified that she is in communication with her husband almost daily, and did not adequately explain why she could not simply ask her husband for more details concerning the news articles and obtain them herself from the sources. I note that the NDP makes multiple references to the media sources the Nation, Vanguard, and the Punch as being major credible Nigerian news sources with Internet sites.
Threatening Letters

[36] The claimant and her counsel listed six threatening letters in the table of contents of the submitted evidence of 24 April 2019. The tribunal only received two photocopies of threatening letters in the documents received dated 24 April 2019. On the day of the hearing, the claimant submitted six original threatening letters with red "X" at the bottom (C-7). One of the threatening letters (C-7.1b), submitted to the tribunal as the original of a photocopy of the same threatening letter already submitted into evidence (C-7.1a), did not match the copy. It is not the same document: C-7.1b has two white triangles in the image of the coffin and the handwritten "X" at the bottom is not the same as in C-7.1a.
[37] I asked the claimant why there was a difference between the two documents. She responded that she did not know.

[38] Asked why she would not have submitted the four other threatening letters on 24 April 2019 with the two others, the claimant responded that the two letters were the ones available to her at the time, and she testified that she or her husband had received five threatening letters together in total, and one letter was found with the dead body of her husband's brother, making a total of six threatening letters.

[39] The claimant's explanation for the difference between C-7.1b and C-7.1a is not adequate, and undermines her credibility and reliability as a witness able to submit original documents in support of photocopy evidence that she submitted. She submitted C-7.1b as the original of C-7.1a, since it is the only threatening letter with a coffin in it and there are only six threatening letters, according to her testimony. However, with C-7.1b and C-7.1a being two separate documents, there are in effect seven threatening letters. Having considered all of the evidence and finding the claimant generally not credible, and with her inadequate explanation for the non-corresponding threatening letter, C-7.1b, I conclude that she has submitted a fraudulent document into evidence in her refugee claim.

[40] Since all of the threatening letters of a similar style and source, because one or more of them is fraudulent, and because the claimant is generally not credible, I do not give any probative value to any of them.
Police report of XXXX XXXX 2018

[41] During the hearing of 8 May 2019, I requested from counsel and the claimant the first pages of C-9, because it appeared that I had only received the last two pages, including the officer's signature at the end on 24 April 2019. Counsel gave me a photocopy of all the pages of C-9 for the refugee file.

[42] At that same sitting of the hearing, the claimant submitted an original police report dated XXXX XXXX 2018 (C-9b), which did not match the photocopy of the same alleged document submitted earlier into evidence (C-9a) sent to our file on 24 April 2019. At the subsequent sitting of the hearing, on 28 May 2019, I mentioned that the two documents do not appear to be the same and asked the claimant first if the original she submitted of C-9 was the same as the photocopy of C-9 that she submitted. She responded that they are the same words, and the one she submitted at the hearing is the true copy of the original and the photocopy was a scanned copy. Asked if the scanned copy of C-9 in our file was a copy of the original, she responded that the scanned copy was not supposed to be used and that the original is the true copy. Asked if there are two versions of the document, the claimant responded that a drink spilled on it and another one was done.

[43] Asked why she would not have mentioned earlier, on presentation of the original of C-9, that the original was not the same document as the C-9 photocopy, the claimant responded that she should have mentioned it, but did not.

[44] C-9a photocopy had only the last two pages of a four-page document, and the last page was highly pixelated and showed the signature in a different position and the word order of the address at the bottom of the page in a different order compared to the original C-9b. Also, the first three pages of C-9a, which were eventually received in the hearing file on 8 May 2019, were very clear compared to the last signature page, that was highly pixelated on page 4 of C-9a, which does not appear to be from the same document as the first three pages of C-9a, based on the quality of the image, scan or photocopy.

[45] The claimant's explanation for the difference between C-9a and C-9b is not adequate, and undermines her credibility and reliability as a witness able to submit original documents in support of photocopy evidence that she submitted. She submitted C-9b as the original of C-9a, as if they were the same document. Having considered all of the evidence and finding the claimant generally not credible, and with her inadequate explanation of the non-corresponding original, C-9b, I conclude that she has submitted a fraudulent document into evidence in her refugee claim.
Other Documentary Evidence

[46] The claimant submitted a photocopy of her marriage certificate (original not available) and photos of her wedding (C-14 and C-15). I had no particular reason to doubt that the claimant was married as she alleged. The marriage certificate shows that her husband is a XXXX.
[47] Documents referring to her husband's XXXX XXXX or XXXX were submitted (C-4 and C-6). I accept that the claimant's husband is or was a XXXX in Nigeria.

[48] A letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was submitted, dated XXXX XXXX 2019 (C-5), from the XXXX XXXX. The document attests that the claimant's husband can XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria, and that he stopped due to threats or attacks against him and/or his family and recommends protection. The document does not show that the author has independent knowledge of specific attacks and threats against the claimant's husband, other than what her husband would have told the author (XXXX XXXX). Given that, after having considered all of the evidence, I find the claimant generally not credible and some of her evidence fraudulent, and related to events directly involving the claimant's husband, I conclude that the husband is not a reliable or credible witness. Consequently, since it has not been shown that the XXXX XXXX is relying on information other than the declaration of the husband, I conclude that the XXXX letter does not have any probative value.

[49] The claimant submitted an affidavit from her husband dated XXXX XXXX 2019 (C-13), where he alleges that his brother was assassinated by unknown gunmen. For the reasons stated above for finding the claimant's husband not reliable or credible as a witness, I find that his affidavit does not have any probative value.

[50] The death certificate of the husband's brother (C-3) does not show the cause of death, and is not probative evidence that the cause of the death was the aggressors that the claimant alleges are threatening her. The alleged photo of the brother-in-law (C-16) relies on the claimant's testimony describing the photo as being that of her assassinated brother-in-law, and since I find her generally not credible as a witness, the photo does not have any probative value as proof of the brother's violent death or that he was killed by the same aggressors targeting the claimant.

[51] The claimant submitted a photo (C-8) of her husband with a bandage over his right eye. The claimant testified that her husband was attacked by the aggressors targeting them and he nearly lost an eye. The photo on its own is not probative evidence of the cause of the injury and since the cause of the injury relies on the claimant's explanation of the cause and, after having considered all of the evidence, I find her generally not credible, the photo does not have probative as evidence in support of her allegations.

[52] The signing officer's name in C-9 is XXXX, and the Nigerian police stamp that appears at the bottom of the last page also appears in the death report to the coroner for the husband's brother's death (C-2). Since I conclude that C-9 is a fraudulent document and the signing officers are the same in C-2 as in C-9, I do not give any probative value to C-2.

[53] I note that the NDP mentions that fraudulent documents are common in Nigeria1 in relation to fake news, affidavits from the court, and corrupt state officials. Therefore, in conjunction with the claimant's general lack of credibility, there is serious reason to doubt the credibility and probative value of the submitted documents.
Claim is Manifestly Unfounded

[54] Section 107.1 of the IRPA reads:
"If the Refugee Protection Division rejects a claim for refugee protection, it must state in its reasons for the decision that the claim is manifestly unfounded if it is of the opinion that the claim is clearly fraudulent."

[55] I understand "clearly fraudulent" to include where a refugee claimant is deliberately attempting to deceive the tribunal in a refugee claim. I do not consider that a claim is "clearly fraudulent" if, in spite of false statements from a claimant, there is other credible and probative evidence showing the well-foundedness of the claim. I consider that the claimant's false allegations or misrepresentation of alleged fact must be material or of substantive nature relevant to the claim, in order for the claim to be considered "clearly fraudulent".

[56] After having considered the totality of the evidence (the claimant's testimony, personal written statements, and other evidence), I conclude that the claimant is generally not credible as a witness. For the reasons already stated above, I find that the documentary evidence is insufficiently credible and probative to support the claimant's allegations of past and future harm in Nigeria.

[57] In particular, I consider that the claimant has submitted fraudulent documents, either documents that are fake, or authentic documents created in a fraudulent manner and not according to accepted laws or rules of a country. She has submitted a threatening letter from her alleged aggressors (C-7.1b) that she alleged was the origin of her earlier submitted photocopy of the same document, but it was not. The threatening letters are a central element in her claim relating to her alleged main aggressors. She also submitted a police report (C-9b) as the original of a similar document (C-9a), but that did not correspond to the photocopy of C-9a. This police report was one of only two police reports submitted regarding the central allegations of the claim. The claimant's explanation for submitting these originals as the documents corresponding to the copies already submitted was not reasonable or credible.

[58] I conclude from the above that the claimant intentionally attempted to deceive the panel regarding documentary evidence central and material to the claim, and that her claim is clearly fraudulent and manifestly unfounded.
CONCLUSION

[59] I therefore reject your claim under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA, and I further find that your claim is manifestly unfounded pursuant to section 107.1 of the IRPA.
